texts.title: Ibn Battuta: A Life on the Road
texts.body:
In 1325, a young man of twenty-one left his home in Tangier, in Morocco. His name was Ibn Battuta, and he wanted to perform the Hajj in Mecca. He did not know then that he would not return home for almost twenty-five years.

After the Hajj, Ibn Battuta decided to keep traveling. He visited Egypt, Syria, Iraq and Persia, and later he sailed along the coast of East Africa. In the 1330s he traveled across Anatolia, where he stayed with groups of young men called the Akhis. He wrote that they welcomed strangers into their lodges, gave them food and a place to sleep, and never asked for money. From Anatolia he went on to Central Asia, India and even China.

His journeys were not always safe. He was attacked by robbers, he lost everything he owned when his ships sank, and he was sometimes ill for weeks. However, he also met rulers, scholars and ordinary people, and he worked as a judge in India and in the Maldives.

When he finally came back to Morocco, the sultan asked him to describe his travels. A young scholar, Ibn Juzayy, wrote down his stories, and the book became known as the Rihla. Historians believe that Ibn Battuta traveled more than 100,000 kilometers, more than almost any other person before the age of trains and steamships. Today his book is still one of the most important sources for life in the fourteenth-century Muslim world.

texts.title: Saturdays at the Community Kitchen
texts.body:
Last year my aunt asked me to help at the community kitchen in our neighborhood. I said yes, but to be honest, I only wanted to make her happy. I thought I would be bored, and I was a little nervous about meeting strangers.

On my first Saturday I washed dishes for three hours. My hands were red and my back hurt. But at lunchtime something changed. An old man thanked me for the soup and told me about his life. He used to be a teacher, and he still remembered the names of all his students. I listened to him for half an hour and forgot about the time.

Now I go to the kitchen every Saturday. I have learned how to cook for sixty people, and I have made friends of all ages. My English has improved too, because two of the volunteers come from other countries and we often speak English together.

Some of my friends say that volunteering is a waste of time and that students should study for exams instead. I understand them, but I don’t agree. I study on Sundays, and Saturday is the day I feel most useful. If you are not sure, try it once. You might be surprised, just like I was.

Zeynep, 16

writing.instructions: Write an article for your school website about a person you admire.
prompts: Who is the person? It can be someone from history or from your family.
What did he or she do?
Why do you admire this person?

parts.title: Part 1: Questions about you
parts.instructions: The teacher asks you some questions. Give reasons and examples in your answers.
prompts: What do you like doing in your free time? Why?
Tell me about a person who is important to you.
What is the best way to learn new words in English?
What would you like to do after you finish school?

parts.title: Part 2: Talk about a journey
parts.instructions: Talk for about two minutes about a journey you remember. Then answer one question.
prompts: Where did you go, and why?
What did you learn from it?
Follow-up question: Do you prefer traveling with your family or with friends? Why?
